transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks for seeing me. Um, so, the main thing that really pushed me to finally make an appointment and come in today is... well, it's about my job, honestly. I work as an insurance claims clerk, so I do a lot of policy processing, which, as you can probably guess, means I spend pretty much my entire day sitting in front of a dual-monitor setup just staring at spreadsheets and claim forms. 

And the problem is, I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. I’ll be right in the middle of a batch of files—and we have these quotas we're supposed to hit, so I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish my claim reviews—but I just find myself walking away from my desk. I'll get up to go to the breakroom to fill my water bottle even if it's already full, or I'll just walk down the hall, or I'll go over to someone else's cubicle to ask a question that definitely could have just been an instant message. 

It’s like, I know I need to stay in my chair, the work is right there on my screen, and I tell myself, "Okay, just sit here until this stack is done," but I just... I can't seem to stay glued to the seat. I just keep leaving my desk, and it's really starting to become a noticeable issue with my productivity. My supervisor hasn't formally written me up yet, but I can tell she's noticing that I'm never at my desk when she walks by, so I figured I really needed to talk to a doctor about it before it turns into a bigger deal.
Outside of having trouble staying seated, do you often find it difficult to keep your focus on tasks that require sustained mental effort?

Oh, yeah, definitely. That’s actually a huge part of the problem, maybe even more than the walking around. When I log into our system in the morning, I get this daily queue of claims, right? And you can sort of tell right away just by looking at the coding which ones are going to be a massive headache. 

If I see a file in there that I know is going to need a really long written explanation, or if it's one of those complicated ones where I have to dig in and check a bunch of dense policy language to see what's actually covered... I just, I can't even bring myself to open it. I’ll look at it and my brain just sort of goes, "Nope, not right now, we can't handle that." 

So I’ll tell myself, "Okay, I'll just knock out the easy ones first to build some momentum." And then I’ll just spend hours doing all these really easy, quick tasks—like simple address updates or basic approvals that just take two clicks. I'll just keep putting off the hard ones, bypassing them in the queue, telling myself I'll get to them after lunch, or after my next break, until suddenly it's 4:30 and I'm basically out of time for the day. And then those complicated files just sit there, and I have to roll them over to the next day, which really messes up my turnaround time metrics. It's like the second I realize a task is going to take actual, heavy brainpower and I really have to think, I just find any excuse to avoid it and do the easy stuff instead.

Like, he'll text me at 11 at night freaking out about whether he left his stove on, or if he said the wrong thing to his girlfriend's dad three weeks ago, or what if the economy crashes and he loses his job. He just spirals about all these hypothetical things that haven't even happened and probably won't happen. 

I'm not like that at all. I don't really lay awake at night agonizing over, I don't know, my health, or getting into a car crash, or the future, or anything like that. My brain doesn't really latch onto worries like that. If anything, my problem is that my brain won't latch onto the things it *should* be focusing on, like those complicated claims files I was telling you about. But yeah, as far as just general, constant worrying about life stuff or bad things happening? No, that's not really something I deal with. I'm generally pretty chill about things outside of the immediate frustration of just not being able to get my work done right.
Do you frequently make careless mistakes or miss important details when working on tasks or paperwork?

Um, careless mistakes? No, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, sure, everyone makes a typo now and then, but I'm actually pretty careful when I finally do sit down and do the work. It's more about just getting myself to do it, you know? Like I was saying with the easy claims versus the hard ones. Once I'm actually looking at the file and entering the data, I'm not, like, putting in the wrong policy numbers or approving things that shouldn't be approved or missing big chunks of information. 

Our system actually has a lot of built-in checks, too, so it's kind of hard to make a really massive mistake without a pop-up yelling at you, but even before that, I'm pretty thorough. I think because I know I struggle to focus, when I *am* focused, I almost overcompensate by double-checking things? Like, I'll read the same line in a policy manual three times just to make sure my brain actually absorbed it, rather than just skimming it and making a bad call. So, yeah, I don't really get dinged on quality assurance reviews for errors or missing details. My accuracy rating is actually really good, usually around 98 or 99 percent. It's just the volume and the time it takes me to get through the queue that's the problem, not the quality of the work itself. So, no, not really careless mistakes.

Yeah, actually, I do that a lot. It's funny you ask that because I don't really notice it myself half the time until someone points it out, or until I'm in a situation where I'm really trying to hold still. 

Like, when we have these mandatory training sessions—they do these quarterly updates on compliance and new state regulations, and they drag everyone into this big conference room on the third floor. The chairs in there are those really stiff, ergonomic ones that are actually horribly uncomfortable if you sit in them for more than ten minutes. Anyway, when I'm in those trainings, or even just during our longer weekly team meetings where the supervisor goes over the metrics and all that, I am constantly moving. 

I'll be sitting there, and my leg will just be going a mile a minute, just bouncing up and down under the table. Or I'll have a pen—I always try to bring a clicky pen with me, which is probably a bad idea in hindsight—and I'll just be clicking it, click-click-click, just over and over. I had a coworker actually lean over once during a presentation on Medicare Part D and ask me to stop because the clicking was driving her crazy. I hadn't even realized I was doing it! 

And even when I try to stop the clicking or the leg bouncing, I just can't seem to stay settled in the chair. I'm always shifting my weight, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. I try so hard to look like I'm paying attention and focused on whoever is talking, especially if it's the department head, but my body just feels like it has this nervous energy that has to go somewhere. It's almost like if I don't move some part of me, I'm going to jump out of my skin. So yeah, the tapping and shifting around is definitely a constant thing for me whenever I'm stuck in a chair for too long.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by noises, activity around you, or unrelated thoughts when you are trying to work?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's honestly one of the biggest reasons I struggle with those complicated claims files I mentioned earlier. Our office setup is this open-plan thing, which I guess was supposed to foster collaboration or whatever, but for me, it's just a nightmare of distractions. 

Like, if I'm trying to read through a really dense medical history report—one of those ones where you have to cross-reference dates of service with the specific billing codes to make sure they aren't double-dipping—and the people in the pod next to me start talking about a claim they're working on, it's game over. Even if it's work-related, even if they're just discussing a routine dental pre-auth, my brain just completely abandons what I'm doing and latches onto their conversation. I'll be sitting there staring at my screen, but I'm actually listening to them debate whether a root canal was medically necessary. 

And it's not just other people, either. It's my own brain. I'll be right in the middle of a sentence in a policy document, and suddenly I'll remember, like, "Oh, I need to pick up dry cleaning," or "Did I ever reply to my mom's text about Sunday dinner?" or even just some random trivia fact I read on Reddit three days ago. And once that unrelated thought pops in, my attention just completely slides right off what I'm reading. 

It's so frustrating because I'll realize I've been staring at the same paragraph for five minutes, and I have no idea what it says. I end up having to reread the exact same section three, four, maybe five times before the information actually sticks and I can process what it means for the claim. It's like my focus is covered in Teflon or something, nothing sticks to it if there's even the slightest bit of noise or a random thought passing through my head. So yeah, distractibility is a huge, huge issue for me all day long.
Do you often feel like you are 'on the go' or driven by an internal motor, finding it uncomfortable to remain still for extended periods?

Driven by a motor? Um... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it's kind of the exact opposite most of the time. 

I know I just said I fidget a lot and bounce my leg during those meetings, but that's more of a nervous, trapped energy when I'm stuck in a chair and bored out of my mind. It's definitely not like I have this endless supply of energy or feel like I need to be running around doing things. Honestly, by the time I get off work at 5:00, I am completely wiped out. Like, mentally and physically drained just from trying to force myself to focus on those claims files all day. I'll get home to my apartment, and I just crash on the couch. 

I'm definitely not one of those people who goes to the gym after work or, you know, joins a recreational softball league or anything like that. My roommate, he's exactly like what you're describing—he's always doing something, always has to be out of the house on weekends, going hiking or to a brewery or just driving around because he can't sit still. He's always asking me to go do stuff, but me? I'm totally fine just staying in. If I don't have mandatory errands to run, I could easily just sit on the couch all Saturday playing video games or watching two-hour-long YouTube video essays. I don't get that restless "I need to go do an activity" feeling at all. 

It's more just... I can't focus on the things I'm *supposed* to do, but I'm perfectly content being physically still if I'm doing something I actually want to do, like gaming. So, yeah, "driven by a motor" doesn't really sound like me. I'm probably more of a stalling engine, if anything. Just really sluggish when it comes to getting moving on things, rather than always being on the go.

Oh man, yeah. Organization is... it's a total disaster area right now, to be completely honest. It used to be somewhat manageable, I guess, but recently my caseload got a lot bigger. They shifted some territories around because one of the other clerks transferred to a different department, so suddenly I'm dealing with a much higher volume of claims.

And my inbox—don't even get me started on my email. I try to use the little colored flags in Outlook, you know? Like, I'll flag something red if it's urgent, or yellow if we're waiting on provider records. But now I have so many emails coming in that almost everything is flagged, so the flags mean absolutely nothing. It's just a giant wall of red. 

So when I sit down in the morning, I just stare at it all, and I have such a hard time figuring out which policy review to actually tackle first. Like, do I start with the oldest ones to get them out of the queue? Or the ones that have the highest dollar amount? Or the ones where the claimant keeps calling customer service to complain? I'll spend, like, forty-five minutes just shuffling the physical folders around, moving a pile from the left side of my keyboard to the right side, and then looking at my flagged emails, trying to make a master to-do list. But by the time I write the list, I've completely lost the train of thought for the very first file. It's just this constant cycle of trying to get organized, making a bigger mess, and then feeling totally paralyzed because I can't prioritize what needs my attention first. My supervisor keeps telling me I need a better "system," but every time I try to build one, it just falls apart because there are too many moving pieces.

Forgetful? Oh man, yeah. That’s... yeah, that’s actually a huge problem for me right now. Especially at work. I forget these really simple work follow-ups way, way more than I want to admit. It’s actually getting kind of embarrassing, to be honest.

It's literally just typing a quick sentence, like "reviewed medicals, pending supervisor approval." But I will do the entire review, spend twenty minutes squinting at a doctor's terrible handwriting, figure out exactly what needs to happen, and then... I just close the file. I completely forget to type the actual note. So the system thinks the file hasn't been touched in a week, and it flags it as overdue, even though I literally did the work! My supervisor pulls these metric reports on Fridays, and she's always asking why my diary notes are missing, and I just... I don't know, it just completely slips my mind the exact second I finish reading the document. 

Or I'll forget to send a form that I fully meant to send earlier that day. Like, if we need a claimant to fill out a specific medical release form so we can request records from their orthopedic surgeon. I'll actually draft the whole email. I'll type out "Dear Mr. Johnson, please find attached..." and I'll have the cursor right there, ready to go. I go to the intranet, maybe get distracted by some corporate newsletter on the homepage, or maybe Dave two pods down starts talking about his dog again, and I just leave the draft sitting there minimized on my taskbar. I'll go home at 5:00, feeling like I had a somewhat productive day, and then the next morning I log into my computer and see this unsent draft just staring at me. It's incredibly frustrating because the work is like 99% done, but I just forget that last crucial step of actually attaching the form and hitting send. So, yeah, daily activities, especially those little routine steps at my job... they just evaporate from my brain constantly.

Losing things? Yeah... yeah, that is a massive, massive daily struggle for me. It’s actually ridiculous how much time I spend every single day just... hunting for things I literally just had in my hands a second ago. It’s like my workspace has this invisible black hole on it. 

Take my headset, for example. I have to wear this wireless headset for the claimant calls, right? And sometimes I’ll take it off just for a second to rub my ears, or maybe I’ll stand up to stretch my legs while I’m reading a long, boring policy document on my monitor. I will set the headset down, and I swear to you, I don't even leave my cubicle, but when a call comes in two minutes later and the software starts beeping, I cannot find it. I’ll be tearing through my desk drawers, looking under my chair, lifting up stacks of paper in a total panic, and I’ll eventually find it resting on top of the filing cabinet behind me, and I have absolutely zero memory of turning around and putting it there. 

And it’s even worse with paperwork and notes. If the main database is lagging, which it does all the time, I’ll jot down a claimant’s callback number on a sticky note so I don't lose it. I’ll stick it right to the plastic edge of my monitor. Or at least, I think I do. But then I’ll go to actually make the call, and the sticky note is just gone. Did it fall? Did I accidentally throw it away with my lunch wrapper? I’ll spend twenty minutes moving every single object on my desk trying to find this one little yellow square of paper. Half the time I find it stuck to the bottom of my coffee mug, or stuck to the back of a completely unrelated printed claim form that I was reviewing. 

Speaking of claim forms, I lose those constantly, too. If I have to print out a physical faxed appeal to highlight the medical codes—because sometimes squinting at them on the screen gives me a headache—I will somehow manage to lose the physical paper between the communal printer and my desk. And it’s not even just desk stuff, it’s my access badge to even get into the building. I’m supposed to keep it clipped to my belt on one of those retractable lanyards, but I’ll take it off to scan into the parking garage gate from my car window. I’ll toss it onto the passenger seat, completely forgetting that I need it to actually open the glass doors to the lobby. So I’ll get all the way up to the front doors, my coffee in one hand, my bag in the other, and realize I don't have my badge. I either have to do the walk of shame all the way back out to the parking garage, or I have to stand there awkwardly waiting for someone from the underwriting department to walk by and badge me in. They all know me by now, too, which is just embarrassing. It’s just... I’m constantly, constantly searching for the basic tools I need to just exist and do my job. It’s exhausting, honestly.
